newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish Nov credit growth 16.4 pct y/y - Central Bank.
newsitem.headline: Irish Nov credit growth 16.4 pct y/y - Central Bank.

text.p: The adjusted annual rate of growth of Irish private sector credit rose to 16.4 percent in November from a revised 14.4 percent in October, central bank monthly statistics showed on Thursday.
The bank said the increase in private sector credit was entirely Irish-pound denominated and mainly non-mortgage.
Non-mortgage Irish pound credit rose to 17.5 percent from 14.2 percent while the annual rate of increase in residential mortgage lending by all credit institutions was unchanged at 17.1 percent.

A rise of 214 million punts in lending to the Agricultural Intervention Agency contributed to the strong rise in non-mortgage lending and excluding this factor, the November increase would have been 16.7 percent, the bank said.

"As lending to the Agency increased by only 79 million in November 1995, this factor made a significant contribution to the acceleration in the year-on-year rate of credit growth," the central bank said.
Borrowing to fund tax payments also appeared to have contributed to the rise in Irish-pound credit in November.
Overall, private sector credit rose by 389 million or 1.2 percent in November.
This was entirely due to the strength of Irish-pound lending which increased by 746 million, the central bank said.

Foreign currency credit fell by 357 million of which 215 million was related to Dublin's International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). The fall was largely due to a reclassification of some lending, the bank said.
Residential mortgage lending rose by 124 million punts, broadly in line with the average monthly rate of increase so far this year while other mortgage increased by 48 million.
The adjusted rate of broad money supply growth (M3E) also rose to 13.6 percent at end-November from 12.4 percent. This represented an increase of 373 million punts or 1.1 percent, the bank said.
Around two-thirds of the increase was Irish-pound denominated while the foreign currency component rose by 140 million.
The increase in the Irish pound component was due mainly to a rise in term deposits with current account and demand deposit account balances both falling.
